n: Hezekiah responds to the threats with humility: he tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and goes to the temple. This time his first move is toward the Lord. (This chapter parallels Isaiah 37.)

f.w: went into the house of the LORD

f.g: rough cloth worn in mourning and repentance.

n: He sends his top officials and senior priests, all in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah. In crisis, the king seeks the Lord’s prophet.

f.w: Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz

n: Hezekiah’s message uses a vivid image: the nation is like a woman in labor with no strength to give birth—the moment of deliverance has come, but they are powerless to bring it about.

f.g: punishment, reproach.

f.w: the children are come to the birth

n: He hopes the Lord has heard the Rabshakeh mock “the living God”—in contrast to lifeless idols—and asks Isaiah to pray for the surviving remnant.

f.g: insult, taunt.
those left after Assyria’s conquest of Judah’s towns.

n: The officials deliver the message to Isaiah.
Isaiah’s reply begins with comfort: “Do not be afraid.” The Assyrians have insulted not just Judah but the Lord Himself.
The Lord will put a “spirit” in Sennacherib so that a rumor sends him home, where he will die by the sword. This is fulfilled in verses 36–37.

f.g: literally ‘a spirit’—a disposition or impulse from God.

f.w: fall by the sword in his own land

n: The Rabshakeh returns to find Sennacherib now fighting at Libnah, having finished with Lachish.

f.g: a fortified town near Lachish.

n: Hearing that Tirhakah, the Cushite (Ethiopian) ruler of Egypt, is marching against him, Sennacherib sends Hezekiah another threat to keep up pressure.

f.g: Taharqa of Egypt’s Cushite (25th) dynasty, from Nubia.

n: Now Sennacherib attacks Hezekiah’s God directly: “Don’t let your God deceive you.”
“You know what Assyria’s kings have done to every land. Will you be the exception?”
He lists cities and peoples in Mesopotamia and Syria that earlier Assyrian kings conquered, whose gods failed them.

f.g: a city in northern Mesopotamia where Abraham once lived.

n: Where are their kings now? All defeated.
Hezekiah takes the letter to the temple and spreads it out before the Lord—a beautiful picture of bringing our burdens directly to God.
His prayer begins with worship: the Lord is enthroned above the cherubim, the only God of all kingdoms, the Creator of heaven and earth.

f.g: enthroned above the cherubim on the ark of the covenant.
cherubim, heavenly beings; the -im ending is already plural in Hebrew.

n: He asks God to listen and look—to see how Sennacherib insults the living God.

f.g: lean down to listen.

n: Hezekiah honestly admits the facts: Assyria really has destroyed many nations.
But their gods were only wood and stone made by human hands, so of course they were burned.
He asks for deliverance not just for Judah’s sake but so all the world will know that the Lord alone is God. The best prayers seek God’s glory.

f.w: that all the kingdoms of the earth may know

n: Isaiah sends word that the Lord has heard Hezekiah’s prayer. What follows is a poem of judgment against Assyria.
Jerusalem is pictured as a young woman who laughs and shakes her head at her would-be attacker. The bully’s threats will come to nothing.

f.w: The virgin the daughter of Zion
f.g: a poetic name for Jerusalem, pictured as an unconquered young woman.
a gesture of scorn.

n: The Lord asks: whom have you insulted? None other than “the Holy One of Israel”—Isaiah’s favorite title for God, which the Book of Mormon also uses often.
The Lord quotes Sennacherib’s boasts: his chariots have conquered mountain heights and felled Lebanon’s finest cedars. Assyrian kings truly did boast of cutting cedars in Lebanon.

f.g: its farthest reaches, its remotest heights.
its most fruitful forest or garden land.

n: He boasts of digging wells in foreign lands and drying up rivers with his feet—claiming power over nature.

f.g: foreign waters.
possibly ‘the streams of Egypt’ (Hebrew matsor).

n: The Lord answers: “Haven’t you heard? I planned this long ago.” Assyria’s conquests were only permitted as part of God’s plan—they were never Assyria’s own power.

f.w: Hast thou not heard long ago

f.g: piles of rubble.

n: Conquered peoples were as weak as grass on a rooftop that withers before it grows.

f.g: grass sprouting on flat clay roofs, which quickly withers.
grain scorched by the hot east wind.

n: The Lord knows everything about Sennacherib—where he sits, goes, and comes, and his raging against God.

f.w: thy going out, and thy coming in

n: Because of his arrogance, the Lord will put a hook in his nose and a bit in his mouth and lead him home—the very way Assyrians led captives.

f.g: Assyrians led captives with hooks through their noses or lips.

n: Now a sign for Hezekiah: for two years they will eat what grows on its own, but in the third year they will plant and harvest normally. Life will return.

f.w: such things as grow of themselves
f.g: self-seeded crops from the previous harvest.

n: The surviving remnant of Judah will put down roots and bear fruit again—a picture of renewal.

f.w: take root downward, and bear fruit upward

n: A remnant will go out from Jerusalem and Mount Zion. “The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this”—a phrase also used in the great messianic prophecy of Isaiah 9.

f.w: the zeal of the LORD of hosts shall do this

n: The Lord promises specifically: Sennacherib will not enter Jerusalem, shoot one arrow, raise a shield, or build a siege ramp against it.

f.g: build a siege ramp.

n: He will go back the way he came.
The Lord will defend Jerusalem for His own name’s sake and for the covenant with David.

That night the angel of the Lord strikes the Assyrian camp, and 185,000 die. Sennacherib’s own records boast of shutting Hezekiah up but never claim to have taken Jerusalem. The ancient historian Herodotus also preserves a story of a sudden disaster striking Sennacherib’s army.

f.w: an hundred fourscore and five thousand
f.g: 185,000; fourscore = eighty.

n: Sennacherib withdraws to his capital, Nineveh, and never returns to Judah.

f.g: the Assyrian capital on the Tigris River, near modern Mosul in Iraq.

n: Years later (681 BC) two of his sons murder him while he worships in his god’s temple, and his son Esarhaddon becomes king. Assyrian and Babylonian records confirm he was assassinated by a son. The god who couldn’t save Sennacherib contrasts with the Lord who saved Jerusalem.

f.g: an otherwise unknown Assyrian god, perhaps a scribal form of Nusku or Marduk.
Hebrew Ararat, the region of Urartu north of Assyria.
king of Assyria 681–669 BC.
